title_content.content: Genome-wide analysis of the SWEET gene family and its response to powdery mildew and leaf spot infection in the common oat (Avena sativa L.)

paragraph_content.content: Yuanbo Pan<sup>1</sup>, Kuiju Niu<sup>1*</sup>, Peiqin Miao<sup>1</sup>, Guiqin Zhao<sup>1</sup>, Yuehua Zhang<sup>2</sup>, Zeliang Ju<sup>3</sup>, Jikuan Chai<sup>1</sup>, Juanjuan Yang<sup>1</sup>, Xiaoning Cui<sup>1</sup> and Ran Zhang<sup>4</sup>

The nutritional quality and yield of oats (Avena sativa) are often compromised by plant diseases such as red leaf, powdery mildew, and leaf spot. Sugars Will Eventually be Exported Transporters (SWEETs) are newly identified sugar transporters involved in regulating plant growth and stress responses. However, the roles of SWEET genes in biotic stress responses remain uncharacterized in oats. In this study, 13 AsSWEET genes were identified across nine chromosomes of the oat genome, all of which were predicted to contain seven transmembrane regions. Phylogenetic analysis revealed four clades of AsSWEET proteins, with high homology to SWEET proteins in the Poaceae family. Collinearity analysis demonstrated strong relationships between oat and Zea mays SWEETs. Using subcellular localization prediction tools, AsSWEET proteins were predicted to localize to the plasma membrane. Promoter analysis revealed cis-acting elements associated with light response, growth, and stress regulation. Six AsSWEET proteins were predicted to interact in a network centered on AsSWEET1a and AsSWEET11. Gene expression analysis of two oat varieties, ‘ForagePlus’ and ‘Molasses’, indicated significant expression diferences in several AsSWEET genes following infection with powdery mildew or leaf spot, including AsSWEET1a, AsSWEET1b, AsSWEET2b, AsSWEET3a, AsSWEET11, and AsSWEET16. These SWEET genes are potential candidates for disease resistance in oats. This study provides a foundation for understanding the regulatory mechanisms of AsSWEET genes, particularly in response to powdery mildew and leaf spot, and ofers insights for enhancing oat molecular breeding.
Keywords SWEET sugar transporter protein, Bioinformatics analysis, Oat, Powdery mildew, Leaf spot

paragraph_content.content: In plants, sugars serve as the primary sources of carbon and energy [1]. Sugars are also known to be important signaling molecules. In mesophyll cells of higher plants, chloroplasts can fix carbon by converting carbon dioxide into organic carbon through photosynthesis [2–4]. However, sugars cannot be transported independently through plant cell membrane systems, requiring the assistance of appropriate sugar transporters [2]. Three main types of sugar transport proteins have been identified: monosaccharide transporters (MSTs) [5], sucrose transporters (SUTs) [6, 7], and Sugars Will Eventually be Exported Transporters (SWEETs) [8]. In the past twenty years, MSTs and SUTs have been widely studied in plants [9]. The SWEET family genes play important roles in transporting hexose and sucrose across cell membranes [10], though their specific functions remain largely unknown.

SWEETs are widely distributed in both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. They are a type of sugar transport protein that does not depend on environmental pH values. Eukaryotic SWEET proteins typically consist of seven alpha-helical transmembrane domains (7-TMs), which are folded into two 3-TM domains (conserved MtN3/ saliva domains) connected by one central TM [11]. SWEETs have been reported to be involved in regulating the response of plants to biotic stress. When plants are invaded by bacterial or fungal pathogens, the pathogens obtain the necessary sugars from the plants, thereby triggering the up-regulation of SWEET gene expression [12, 13]. In the sweet potato, expression of IbSWEET10 was elevated after infection with Fusarium oxysporum Schlecht. f. sp. Batatas; IbSWEET10 overexpression resulted in resistance to this pathogen, and RNAi of IbSWEET10 produced the opposite efect [14]. In Vitis vinifera, VvSWEET4 has been found to interact with the fungal pathogen Botrytis cinerea [15]. GhSWEET42 was found to be up-regulated in Gossypium spp infected with Verticillium dahlia [16]. Overexpression of GhSWEET42 resulted in increased susceptibility, whereas GhSWEET42 deficiency increased resistance. Similarly, in V. vinifera, VvSWEET7 expression was induced by pathogens, contributing to plant defense via removal of pathogen-synthesized mannitol from the apoplast [17]. The roles of endogenous sugars in mediating plant immune responses and combating pathogen attacks are receiving increasing attention, leading to the emergence of concepts such as “sweet immunity” or “sugar enhanced defense” [18, 19]. Regulating these sugar levels will be significant for crop improvement.

Oats (Avena sativa) are an important annual cereal and feed crop in the Poaceae family [20]. Due to their strong stress resistance, excellent quality, high yield, good palatability, easy harvesting, and straightforward processing and modulation, oats are a globally cultivated crop [21]. Oats are mainly produced in Russia, Canada, the United States, Australia, Germany, Finland, China, and several other nations in the northern hemisphere [22]. Global population growth and the increasing demand for nutritious and healthy foods have led to annual increases in oat production [23]. With changes in climate and environmental conditions, oat cultivation has been threatened by diseases such as powdery mildew, red leaf disease, smut, and leaf spot, which have inhibited the quality and yield of oats in recent years [24, 25]. Currently, fungal plant diseases in oats are controlled using methods such as field cultivation management, biological control, chemical control, and the breeding of resistant varieties [26]. However, cultivation management is timeconsuming and labor-intensive, and chemical control can easily lead to environmental pollution [27]. Thus, the identification and characterization of genes involved in disease susceptibility and resistance are necessary to provide a basis for the genetic improvement of crops.

Thus far, numerous studies have shown that SWEET sugar transporters are closely associated with biotic and abiotic stress responses in plants [28–30], but few of these studies have characterized the roles of oat SWEETs in response to biotic stress. Therefore, this study aimed to identify the oat SWEET family genes and systematically analyze the structural characteristics, conserved protein motifs and structures, and the expression of these SWEET genes in oat leaves under diferent disease stresses. This study provides a theoretical basis for understanding the role of SWEET genes in regulating plant disease resistance, thereby facilitating the exploration of superior oat genetic resources and the development of new cultivars.

title_content.content: Identification and analysis of physicochemical properties of oat SWEET genes

paragraph_content.content: Using comparative approaches, 13 SWEET genes were identified in the oat genome. AsSWEET gene names were assigned based on close evolutionary relationships to previously annotated SWEET genes in closely related species. These were named AsSWEET1a, AsSWEET1b, AsSWEET2a, AsSWEET2b, AsSWEET3a, AsSWEET4, AsSWEET5, AsSWEET11, AsSWEET12, AsSWEET13, AsSWEET15, AsSWEET16, and AsSWEET17. The AsS-WEETs were distributed across nine chromosomes (Fig.  1). These genes encoded proteins ranging from 231 (AsSWEET2b) to 313 (AsSWEET16) amino acids in length, with an average of about 267 amino acids and molecular weights ranging from 25.4  kDa to 34.1  kDa (Table  1). title_content.content: Predictions of AsSWEET protein secondary and tertiary structures

paragraph_content.content: The secondary structures of all 13 AsSWEET proteins were predicted to contain α-helices, irregular curls, β-turns, and extension chains, though the proportions of each structure varied (Additional file 1: Table S1, Additional file 1: Fig. S1). For all AsSWEET proteins, α-helices were the largest contributors to their secondary structures. The proportions of irregular curly structures ranged from 28.68 to 39.70%, with an average of

33.59%. β-turn structures were the smallest contributors in all AsSWEET proteins. The proportions of extended chains fluctuated, ranging from 13.74 to 25.30%. Predictions of tertiary structures of AsSWEET proteins (Fig. 2) indicated that the tertiary structures of AsSWEET1a and AsSWEET1b were highly similar, as were the tertiary structures of AsSWEET2a and AsSWEET2b. The predicted tertiary structures of the remaining proteins had significant diferences, though α-helical structures were the main structural component in all.

Motif lengths ranged between 6 and 50 amino acids, with motif l and motif 2 both 50 amino acids in length (Additional file 1: Fig. S2). Motif 11 and motif 12 were both 26 amino acids in length, while motifs 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, and 10 had lengths of 31, 22, 21, 32, 8, 20, 6, and 7 amino acids, respectively. In addition, motifs 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8 contained relatively few conserved amino acid residues. Motifs l, 2, 7, 9, 10, 11, and 12 contained multiple conserved amino acid residues, suggesting that they may play important roles in sugar transport in oats. According to NCBI’s Batch CD-search, all oat SWEET proteins contained two conserved domains, with six oat SWEET proteins (AsS-WEET1b, 5, 11, 12, 13, and 15) containing two MtN3_slv conserved domains, three oat SWEETs (AsSWEET2a, 2b, and 17) containing two PQ loop conserved domains, and four oat SWEET proteins (AsSWEET1a, 3a, 4, and 16) each containing one MtN3_slv and one PQ loop conserved domain.

title_content.content: Phylogenetic analysis of SWEET protein sequences

paragraph_content.content: A SWEET family phylogenetic tree was reconstructed using 13 oat sequences, 16 Hordeum vulgare sequences, 17 Arabidopsis thaliana sequences, 21 Oryza sativa sequences, and 24 Zea mays sequences. Phylogenetic analysis indicated that members of the oat AsSWEET protein family were divided into four main clades (Fig. 4). Oat AsSWEETs had high homology with monocotyledonous H. vulgare HvSWEETs, O. sativa OsSWEETs, and Z. mays ZmSWEETs, whereas multiple AtSWEETs proteins from the dicotyledonous A. thaliana clustered independently of the AsSWEETs, HvSWEETs, OsS-WEETs, and ZmSWEETs.

title_content.content: Identification of cis-acting elements in AsSWEETs

paragraph_content.content: The cis-acting elements identified in the promoter regions of the AsSWEETs were associated with light response, growth and development, hormone response, and abiotic stress response (Fig.  5C). All 13 AsSWEET genes contained at least one and up to nine photoresponsive elements. Ten genes contained between one and four auxin-responsive elements, and 12 genes contained between one and four gibberellin-responsive elements. Several genes contained MeJA-responsive elements, salicylic acid responsive elements, and abscisic acid responsive elements (Fig. 5B, C). In addition, AsSWEET17 and AsSWEET12 contained defense and stress response elements. Overall, the promoter regions of these AsSWEETs contained various types of cis-acting regulatory elements, indicating their potential involvement in diverse biological processes and regulatory pathways.

title_content.content: Synteny analysis of SWEET family genes

paragraph_content.content: To explore the evolutionary relationships between AsS-WEETs and SWEETs from other plant species, collinear maps of the oat genome were constructed using three other monocotyledons (H. vulgare, O. sativa, and Z. mays) and one dicotyledon (A. thaliana) (Fig. 6). The AsS-WEET gene family was found to have strong collinearity with SWEET genes from other monocotyledons, with the strongest collinear relationship with O. sativa (9 pairs), followed by H. vulgare (8 pairs) and Z. mays (6 pairs). AsSWEET genes shared a few genes with A. thaliana, the single dicotyledon included in this analysis, including a single syntenic pair of genes. AsSWEET4, AsSWEET16, and AsSWEET17 did not show synteny between oats and any of the four species, suggesting that these genes may have formed after the divergence of plants.

title_content.content: Analysis of AsSWEET expression under biotic stresses Response to powdery mildew

paragraph_content.content: Expression of AsSWEET genes was assayed in two oat cultivars, ‘ForagePlus’ and ‘Molasses’, after inoculation with powdery mildew. ‘ForagePlus’ was more susceptible to powdery mildew than ‘Molasses’. The expression levels of several AsSWEET genes were significantly upregulated or down-regulated after infection (Fig.  8). Expression of AsSWEET1a, 3a, 11, and 16 was significantly up-regulated in the leaves of both cultivars after infection. AsSWEET2a, 2b, and 12 were significantly down-regulated in leaves of ‘ForagePlus’ after infection, while they were significantly up-regulated in ‘Molasses leaves.

title_content.content: Response to leaf spot stress disease

paragraph_content.content: Infection with leaf spot was more severe in ‘Molasses than in ‘ForagePlus’ (Fig.  9). Six days after inoculation, the relative expression levels of AsSWEET1b, 2a, and 2b in ‘ForagePlus’ were significantly increased as compared to the control (p < 0.05). AsSWEET4, 5, 11, 12, 13, 15, and 16 were significantly down-regulated in both cultivars. The expression of AsSWEET17 was stable in ‘ForagePlus’ after infection, while it was significantly down-regulated in leaves of ‘Molasses’.

Sugars serve not only as an energy and carbon source for plant growth and cellular metabolism but also function as important signaling molecules [31–33]. Members of the SWEET sugar transporter protein family regulate the transport and distribution of sugars within cells, across organelles, and between cellular environments, while also playing crucial roles in coordinating plant growth and development under stress conditions [34, 35]. A total of 13 oat AsSWEET family proteins were identified in this study, all of which were predicted to contain 7 TMH structures. Zhang et al. analyzed the SWEET family in Poa pratensis and found that PpSWEET proteins contained 4–7 TMHs (Table 1), consistent with the results of this study [36].

Phylogenetic analysis indicated that the SWEET proteins were divided into four clades. Previous research has shown that SWEETs on diferent phylogenetic branches can transport diferent sugars [37]. SWEETs in Clade I (SWEET1, 2, and 3) and Clade II (SWEET4, 5, 6, 7, and 8) are mainly involved in transporting glucose, fructose, and sucrose. Clade III SWEETs (SWEET9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15) are mainly used for the eficient transport of sucrose [38]. A recent study demonstrated that SWEET14 and SWEET15 are involved in the regulation of hormonal signaling and modulate the plant’s response to gibberellin [39]. Clade IV SWEETs (SWEET16 and 17) are vacuolar membrane transporters, which are primarily used for transporting fructose in leaf and root vacuolar membranes [40]. In this study, oat AsSWEETs were also classified into four clades (Fig. 4), which is consistent with the findings of previous research [40]. In general, similar protein structures imply similar functions. Therefore, it can be inferred that diferent protein members in diferent clades function to transport diferent sugars, though the specific functions of each protein need further empirical validation. The oat AsSWEETs identified here have high genetic similarity with other crops in the Poaceae family. Compared to the dicotyledonous A. thaliana, Poaceae crops do not have SWEET8 and SWEET9, indicating diferences in the evolution of the SWEET gene family in monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous plants.

paragraph_content.content: Salicylic acid can inhibit the activity of plant cell wall degrading enzymes secreted by pathogens, thereby reducing their pathogenicity. Salicylic acid can also induce the expression of disease related genes [41]. Several AsSWEET genes, including AsSWEET1a, 1b, 2a, 2b, and 16, were found to contain salicylic acid responsive cis-regulatory elements (Fig.  5). These genes were differentially expressed after powdery mildew and leaf spot infection stress, indicating that salicylic acid may mediate the resistance of oats to these diseases.

The main energy source for most pathogens is sugar. Plants are known to regulate sugar contents by up-regulating or down-regulating the expression of the SWEET genes in response to various biotic stresses [42]. In the O. sativa SWEET gene family, OsSWEET11, OsSWEET13, and OsSWEET14 are known susceptibility genes to Candida albicans [43]. In O. sativa varieties containing these genes, the transcription activator–like efectors of Candida albicans can bind to the EBE sites in their promoter regions and induce their expression, thus resulting in O. sativa susceptibility [44]. Gao et al. [45] found that after infection with Rhizoctonia solani, the expression of OsSWEET11 was up-regulated in response to the pathogen, with OsSWEET11 overexpression leading to heightened disease susceptibility and mutation resulting in resistance. Zhang et al. [46] found that when potato leaves were infected with late blight, the expression of StSWEET5 was up-regulated, indicating that StSWEET5 may play a role in resistance to this disease. In this study, significant up-regulation of AsSWEET5 was observed in both ‘ForagePlus’ and ‘Molasses’ cultivars three days after powdery mildew infection (Fig.  8), though AsSWEET5 expression was down-regulated at a comparable time point after leaf spot infection (Fig. 9). These results indicate that AsSWEET5 may be involved in the response to both powdery mildew and leaf spot infections, thought the response mechanisms may difer. In A. thaliana infected with clubroot, AtSWEET11 and AtSWEET12 were found to facilitate the transport of sugars toward the pathogen, with disease progression inhibited in AtS-WEET11 and AtSWEET12 double mutants [47]. Fan et al. [48] found that overexpression of StSWEET16b inhibited the expansion of late blight bacteria, thus enhancing disease resistance. In this study, AsSWEET16 was significantly up-regulated after powdery mildew infection (Fig. 8), indicating that AsSWEET16 may be involved in regulating powdery mildew resistance in oats. This study also found that AsSWEET1a, 1b, 2b, 3a, 11, and 16 were either significantly up- or down-regulated after infection with powdery mildew or leaf spot disease (Figs. 8 and 9). Thus, these genes are promising candidates for the regulation of resistance to oat diseases.

paragraph_content.content: In this study, a total of 13 SWEET sugar transporter proteins were identified in the oat, distributed across nine chromosomes in the oat genome. All AsSWEET sugar transporters were predicted to be hydrophobic proteins containing 7 TMHs. Both secondary and tertiary structure predictions indicated α-helices as the main structural components of the AsSWEET proteins. Phylogenetic analysis indicated that AsSWEET proteins clustered into four subfamilies, with high homology to the SWEET protein families of multiple crops in the Poaceae family. AsSWEET promoter regions contained cis-acting elements related to light response, growth and development, and stress response. SWEET genes from oats and O. sativa were found to have strong collinear relationships. Six AsSWEET proteins were predicted to interact with each other in a network centered around AsSWEET1a and AsSWEET11. The AsSWEETs actively participated in the response to biological stress. Among them, AsSWEET1a, 1b, 2b, 3a, 11, and 16 were diferentially expressed after infection with either powdery mildew or leaf spot, making them important candidate genes for studying the oat response to biological stress.

paragraph_content.content: Two oat cultivars that difer in their susceptibility to powdery mildew and leaf spot infection, ‘Avena sativa cv. ForagePlus’ and ‘Avena sativa cv. Molasses’, were used in this study. Seeds of ‘ForagePlus’ and ‘Molasses’ were purchased from Beijing Rytway Seed Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China) and CLOVER (Beijing, China), respectively. The pathogenic fungi of powdery mildew (Blumeria graminis f.sp. avenae) and leaf spot disease (Drechslera avenacea) were isolated and stored by our laboratory.

The protein sequences of SWEET genes in A. thaliana, O. sativa, H. vulgare, and Z. mays were directly downloaded from the NCBI database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih. gov/), visited on 6 January 2024, and the oat genome file was downloaded from the GrainGenes database (https:// wheat.pw.usda.gov/GG3/content/avena-sang-download)

[49], visited on 6 January 2024. To identify oat SWEET genes, the BLAST wrapper in TBtools 2.07 [50] was used to align known SWEET genes to the oat genome. The corresponding alleles were removed from the identified genes to obtain final gene sequences. The naming of the AsSWEET genes was based on the reconstructed evolutionary tree, with gene names assigned from previously annotated SWEET genes of closely related species.

Physicochemical properties of AsSWEET protein sequences, including amino acid number, molecular weight, theoretical isoelectric point, instability index, aliphatic index, and total average hydrophilicity, were analyzed using the ExPAsy-ProtParam tool (https:// web.expasy.org/protparam/) [51]. The online tool of TMHMM-2.0 (https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/services/TMHMM-2.0/) was used to predict transmembrane spiral structures [52]. Subcellular localizations were predicted using ProtComp v. 9.0 (http://www.softberry.com/) [53]. Predictions of protein secondary structure were made using SOPMA (https://npsa-prabi.ibcp. fr/cgi-bin/), and predictions of protein tertiary structure were made using SWISS-MODEL (https://swissmodel. expasy.org/) [54–58], visited on 8 January 2024.

Conserved motif analysis of SWEET amino acid sequences in the oat were performed using the online tool MEME (http://meme-suite.org/) [59], visited on 8 January 2024. Gene structure and motif distributions were visualized using TBtools 2.07 [60]. The maximum likelihood method in MEGA 11.0 was used to construct a SWEET family phylogenetic tree using 13 oat sequences, 16 H. vulgare sequences, 17 A. thaliana sequences, 21 O. sativa sequences, and 24 Z. mays sequences. The protein sequences of the oat, H. vulgare, A. thaliana, O. sativa, and Z. mays used can be found in Additional file 2.

The cis-acting elements in the putative promoter regions of the AsSWEETs, defined as the 2,000  bp upstream of the genes, were predicted using PlantCARE (http://bioinformatics.psb.ugent.be/webtools/plantcare/html/), and TBtools 2.07 was used to visualize predicted cis-acting elements [61].

title_content.content: Chromosome distributions, gene duplication, and collinearity analysis

paragraph_content.content: The visualization of chromosomal localizations of the SWEET genes was performed using TBtools 2.07 [60]. The genome sequences of H. vulgare, A. thaliana, O. sativa, and Z. mays, as described above, were used for collinearity analysis, with Circos 0.69 and TBtools 2.07 used for visualization [62]. The online tool string (https:// cn.string-db.org) was used to predict protein-protein interactions in SWEETs and visualize the results [63], visited on 12 January 2024.

title_content.content: Oat growth conditions and biotic stress treatments

paragraph_content.content: The seeds of two oat cultivars, ‘ForagePlus’ and ‘Molasses’, were sown in plastic pots containing a mixed medium (soil and vermiculite, 2:1). The daytime temperature of growth chambers was 25℃, and the nighttime temperature was 20℃. Oats were grown using a 14-hour light: 10-hour dark cycle. Three replicates were generated for each treatment (control and inoculated). Twenty days after planting, the plants were inoculated with Blumeria graminis f.sp. avenae or Drechslera avenacea by the spore suspension method. Blumeria graminis f.sp. avenae conidia were collected from infected wheat leaves using a fine camel hair brush and suspended in sterile distilled water (containing 0.05% Tween 20) to a concentration of
conidia/mL. A spore suspension of Drechslera avenacea was prepared by first cultivating the fungus on potato dextrose agar (PDA) plates at
2 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \dot { C }

for 10–12 days until sporulation was abundant. The spores were then harvested by flooding the plates with sterile distilled water containing 0.05% Tween 20 and gently scraping the surface with a sterile glass rod. The spore suspension was filtered through a double layer of cheesecloth to remove mycelial fragments and adjusted to a concentration of 10<sup>5</sup> conidia/mL. The conidial suspension was applied to oat plants using a fine mist spray bottle, ensuring complete coverage of foliage. Inoculated plants were incubated at 25 °C with 80–90% relative humidity for 48 h to promote infection, then maintained at 60% humidity. After this incubation period, plants were monitored for development of symptoms, and leaves were sampled at 1 d, 3 d, 6 d, 9 d, and 12 d. Leaves sampled before incubation (0 d) were used as the control. The sampled leaves were immediately frozen in liquid nitrogen and then stored at -80 °C for later RNA extraction.

title_content.content: RNA extraction and real-time quantitative PCR analysis

paragraph_content.content: RNA extraction was performed using the total RNA Extraction Kit (DP419, Tiangen). Then, cDNA was synthesized using the PrimerScript™ RT Reagent Kit with gDNA Eraser (R047A, Takara).

Primers specific for the oat AsSWEET gene were designed using Primer BLAST (https://www.ncbi.nlm. nih.gov/tools/primer-blast/, accessed on 6 January 2024). Primer sequences are shown in Additional file 1: Table S2. qRT-PCR was performed using the SuperReal PreMix Plus (SYBR Green) fluorescence quantification kit. The total 20 µL reaction volume consisted of 5 µL of diluted template (20 µL of cDNA diluted 20-fold with 180 µL of
\mathrm { d d H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } )
, 3 µL of
\mathrm { d d H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } ,

1 µL of upstream and 1 µL of downstream primers (10 µmol·L<sup>-1</sup>), and 10 µL of 2× SuperReal PreMix Plus (SYBR Green). The reaction process was carried out on a LightCycler<sup>Ⓡ</sup>96 instrument. The qRT-PCR reaction procedure was: initial denaturation at 95℃ for 15 min and then 40 cycles of denaturation at 95℃ for 10 s and annealing at 58℃ for 30 s. Three biological replicates were set up for each treatment, and three technical replicates were performed for each biological replicate. The relative gene expression level was calculated using the
2 ^ { - \Delta \Delta \mathrm { C t } }
method [64]. Actin was used as the reference gene.

The Windows version of SPSS 24.0 (SPSS Inc., USA) was used for data analysis, with measurements presented as means with standard errors. Statistical significance between control group and treatment group measurements at diferent times was assessed using t-tests. Figures were drawn using GraphPad Prism 8.0.2 software.
